RIGHT TO REFUSE HAZARDOUS WORK — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

INFORMATION AND BACKGROUND — REFUSAL TO PERFORM WORK BELIEVED HAZARDOUS
I, Jordan Lee, am completing this information sheet in connection with my employment with Acme, Inc., where my job title is Software Engineer. The work I am describing here is: A bronze sculpture titled ‘Pacific Light,’ installed in the plaza in 2015. I believed that performing this work, under the circumstances I describe here, would violate an occupational safety or health standard, a safety order, or a provision of the Labor Code, in a way that would create a real and apparent hazard. I describe that hazard here as: On March 3, 2026, the respondent appeared outside the petitioner’s home and yelled threats for several minutes before leaving. This work was to be performed at 123 Main St., Sacramento, CA, and the date on which I refused to perform it is August 15, 2026. The supervisor or other representative of Acme, Inc. I discussed this with, if any, is Taylor Morgan.

This information sheet describes California Labor Code sections 6310, 6311, and 6312 — statutes addressing an employee's refusal to perform work that would violate an occupational safety or health standard, order, or the Labor Code itself where doing so would create a real and apparent hazard, and a related, broader protection for certain workplace safety complaints and other specified safety-related conduct. This California law applies to employment within California; it does not describe the law of any other state. Completing this sheet is not a complaint or petition. It does not file anything with the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement, the Division of Occupational Safety and Health, the United States Department of Labor, or any court, and does not itself establish that performing the work described above would in fact have violated any safety standard, order, or Labor Code provision, that a real and apparent hazard in fact existed, or that any adverse action taken by Acme, Inc. was connected to the refusal described here. Only the Labor Commissioner, a court, or another body with jurisdiction over a specific complaint can determine whether a violation of these statutes occurred.

THE CORE RIGHT — REFUSING WORK THAT WOULD VIOLATE A SAFETY STANDARD, ORDER, OR THE LABOR CODE ITSELF
California law provides that no employee shall be laid off or discharged for refusing to perform work in the performance of which the Labor Code (including Labor Code section 6400), any occupational safety or health standard, or any safety order of the Division of Occupational Safety and Health or the Occupational Safety and Health Standards Board will be violated, where the violation would create a real and apparent hazard to the employee or the employee's fellow employees. The statute's own text states two conditions, both of which must be present: first, that performing the work would violate the Labor Code itself, an occupational safety or health standard, or a safety order of the division or the standards board; and second, that the violation would create a hazard that is both real and apparent to the employee or a fellow employee. This is a California statute; it does not describe the law of any other state.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "No employee shall be laid off or discharged for refusing to perform work in the performance of which this code, including Section 6400, any occupational safety or health standard, or any safety order of the division or standards board will be violated, where the violation would create a real and apparent hazard to the employee or their fellow employees."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 6311, first sentence (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=6311.)

The quote below was confirmed as an exact (whitespace-normalized) substring of that fetched text. The statute's own text does not itself define the phrase 'real and apparent hazard,' and this research session did not independently verify any published California appellate decision construing that phrase, so this clause states only what the statute's own text says and does not supply a definition beyond it — that is disclosed here as an honest gap rather than filled in with an assumed standard. This document does not itself determine that any specific work would in fact have violated a safety standard, order, or Labor Code provision, or that a real and apparent hazard in fact existed in any specific case.

WHAT THE STATUTE'S OWN TEXT DOES — AND DOES NOT — CONDITION THE RIGHT ON
Labor Code section 6311's own text conditions the right described elsewhere in this document only on the two elements stated in that same text: that performing the work would violate the Labor Code, an occupational safety or health standard, or a safety order of the division or standards board, and that the violation would create a real and apparent hazard to the employee or a fellow employee. The statute's own text does not itself state, as a separate express precondition to that right, that the employee must first have notified the employer of the hazard, asked that it be corrected, or waited any specific period of time before refusing to perform the work.

  — Cal. Labor Code § 6311, first sentence (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=6311.)

None of those secondary sources were independently confirmed in this research session against the text of Labor Code section 6311 itself, against a published California appellate decision construing section 6311, or against any California regulation implementing it, and the federal standard just described is a distinct legal standard under a different, federal statute — not California Labor Code section 6311. This document accordingly does not state a prior-notice precondition, a waiting period, or the federal reasonable-person/imminent-danger standard as if it were part of Labor Code section 6311's own text, and discloses this as an honest, deliberate gap rather than filling it in with an assumed or borrowed standard. This document does not itself determine that a specific employee's conduct did or did not satisfy whatever standard a court or the Labor Commissioner might ultimately apply.

THE REMEDY THE STATUTE ITSELF PROVIDES — A RIGHT OF ACTION FOR WAGES, NOT AUTOMATIC CONTINUED PAY
The same statute provides that an employee who is laid off or discharged in violation of section 6311, or who is otherwise not paid because the employee refused to perform work under the circumstances described elsewhere in this document, has a right of action for wages for the time the employee is without work as a result of the layoff or discharge. This is a right of action — a basis to pursue a legal remedy for the wages lost during that time — rather than a guarantee that an employee who refuses work under this statute automatically continues to receive pay while the refusal is ongoing. Section 6311's protection also extends to a domestic work employee, with a specific exception for a person who performs household domestic service that is publicly funded.

  — Cal. Labor Code § 6311, second sentence (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=6311.)
  "Notwithstanding Section 6303 or other law, as used in this section, “employee” includes a domestic work employee, except for a person who performs household domestic service that is publicly funded, including publicly funded household domestic service provided to a recipient, client, or beneficiary with a share of cost in that service."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 6311, third sentence — domestic work employee (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=6311.)

The statute's own text does not itself state a filing deadline for this right of action; a separate clause of this document addresses the one-year deadline (extendable for good cause) that applies to a Labor Commissioner complaint filed under Labor Code sections 6312 and 98.7, but this document does not assume that the same deadline necessarily governs a right of action for wages framed as a direct civil claim under section 6311 itself, as distinct from that administrative complaint route — this research session did not independently verify a specific limitations period for such a direct claim, and that is disclosed here as an honest gap. This document is informational: it does not itself calculate, determine, or award any specific dollar amount, or determine that a specific layoff, discharge, or nonpayment occurred in violation of this statute in any specific case.

ENFORCEMENT PROCEDURE — A LABOR COMMISSIONER COMPLAINT UNDER SECTIONS 6312 AND 98.7, WITH DEADLINES DISTINCT FROM OTHER RETALIATION CLAIMS
A separate statute provides that an employee who believes they have been discharged or otherwise discriminated against in violation of Labor Code section 6310 or 6311 may file a complaint with the Labor Commissioner. The statute governing that complaint procedure generally allows a complaint to be filed within one year after the occurrence of the violation, a period that may be extended for good cause, and it requires the Labor Commissioner to inform a complainant charging a violation of section 6310 or 6311, at the time of initial contact, of the complainant's right to file a separate, concurrent complaint with the United States Department of Labor within 30 days after the occurrence of the violation. That same procedural statute also provides an appeal path to the Director of Industrial Relations, available specifically for cases arising under sections 6310 and 6311, from a Labor Commissioner determination that would otherwise be final for other categories of claims within the Labor Commissioner's jurisdiction.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]

  — Cal. Labor Code § 6312 (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=6312.)
  "The Labor Commissioner shall inform complainants charging a violation of Section 6310 or 6311, at the time of initial contact, of the complainant’s right to file a separate, concurrent complaint with the United States Department of Labor within 30 days after the occurrence of the violation."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 98.7, subd. (a)(1) — filing deadline and DOL concurrent-complaint notice (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=98.7.)
  "Determinations by the Labor Commissioner under subdivision (c) or (d) shall be final and not subject to administrative appeal except for cases arising under Sections 6310 and 6311, which may be appealed by the complainant to the Director of Industrial Relations pursuant to an appeal process, including time limitations, that is consistent with the mandates of the United States Department of Labor."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 98.7, subd. (e) — appeal to Director of Industrial Relations (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=98.7.)

This document is informational: it does not itself file any complaint, does not determine that a specific complaint would be timely, and does not determine that a violation of Labor Code section 6310 or 6311 occurred in this or any specific case.

A GENUINELY BROADER, SEPARATE PROTECTION — SECTION 6310'S COMPLAINT-BASED PROHIBITION
A separate statute, Labor Code section 6310, prohibits an employer from discharging or in any manner discriminating against an employee because the employee made an oral or written complaint about employee safety or health to the Division of Occupational Safety and Health, another responsible government agency, the employer, or the employer's representative; instituted or participated in a related proceeding; participated in an employer-employee occupational health and safety committee; or reported a work-related fatality, injury, or illness, requested certain injury or illness records, or exercised other rights protected by the federal Occupational Safety and Health Act. This protection is genuinely broader than, and distinct from, the refusal-to-perform-work right described elsewhere in this document: it protects making a safety-related complaint or engaging in the other listed conduct, generally, whether or not the employee ever refused to perform any specific work. An employee who prevails on this protection is entitled to reinstatement and reimbursement for lost wages and work benefits caused by the employer's acts, and an employer who willfully refuses to rehire, promote, or otherwise restore an employee determined eligible for that relief through a grievance procedure, arbitration, or hearing authorized by law is guilty of a misdemeanor. The same statute separately prohibits retaliation against an employee because the employee is a family member of a person who has, or is perceived to have, engaged in conduct this statute protects. This statute's own text expressly excludes from its coverage a case in which the employee alleges retaliation for having filed or made known an intention to file a workers' compensation claim under Labor Code section 132a, which it states is instead under the exclusive jurisdiction of the Workers' Compensation Appeals Board.

Sec. 651 et seq.), except in cases where the employee alleges they have been retaliated against because they have filed or made known their intention to file a workers’ compensation claim pursuant to Section 132a, which is under the exclusive jurisdiction of the Workers’ Compensation Appeals Board."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 6310, subd. (a)(4) — reporting rights and the § 132a/WCAB carve-out (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=6310.)

  — Cal. Labor Code § 6310, subd. (b) — remedy (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=6310.)

expectedJSON.body: A separate statute, Labor Code section 6310, prohibits an employer from discharging or in any manner discriminating against an employee because the employee made an oral or written complaint about employee safety or health to the Division of Occupational Safety and Health, another responsible government agency, the employer, or the employer's representative; instituted or participated in a related proceeding; participated in an employer-employee occupational health and safety committee; or reported a work-related fatality, injury, or illness, requested certain injury or illness records, or exercised other rights protected by the federal Occupational Safety and Health Act. This protection is genuinely broader than, and distinct from, the refusal-to-perform-work right described elsewhere in this document: it protects making a safety-related complaint or engaging in the other listed conduct, generally, whether or not the employee ever refused to perform any specific work. An employee who prevails on this protection is entitled to reinstatement and reimbursement for lost wages and work benefits caused by the employer's acts, and an employer who willfully refuses to rehire, promote, or otherwise restore an employee determined eligible for that relief through a grievance procedure, arbitration, or hearing authorized by law is guilty of a misdemeanor. The same statute separately prohibits retaliation against an employee because the employee is a family member of a person who has, or is perceived to have, engaged in conduct this statute protects. This statute's own text expressly excludes from its coverage a case in which the employee alleges retaliation for having filed or made known an intention to file a workers' compensation claim under Labor Code section 132a, which it states is instead under the exclusive jurisdiction of the Workers' Compensation Appeals Board.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 6310, subd. (a) intro and paragraph (1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: No person shall discharge or in any manner discriminate against any employee because the employee has done any of the following: (1) Made any oral or written complaint to the division, other governmental agencies having statutory responsibility for or assisting the division with reference to employee safety or health, their employer, or their representative.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 6310, subd. (a)(4) — reporting rights and the § 132a/WCAB carve-out (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Reported a work-related fatality, injury, or illness, requested access to occupational injury or illness reports and records that are made or maintained pursuant to Subchapter 1 (commencing with Section 14000) of Chapter 1 of Division 1 of Title 8 of the California Code of Regulations, or exercised any other rights protected by the federal Occupational Safety and Health Act (29 U.S.C. Sec. 651 et seq.), except in cases where the employee alleges they have been retaliated against because they have filed or made known their intention to file a workers’ compensation claim pursuant to Section 132a, which is under the exclusive jurisdiction of the Workers’ Compensation Appeals Board.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 6310, subd. (b) — remedy (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Any employee who is discharged, threatened with discharge, demoted, suspended, or in any other manner discriminated against in the terms and conditions of employment by their employer because the employee has made a bona fide oral or written complaint to the division, other governmental agencies having statutory responsibility for or assisting the division with reference to employee safety or health, their employer, or their representative, of unsafe working conditions, or work practices, in their employment or place of employment, or has participated in an employer-employee occupational health and safety committee, shall be entitled to reinstatement and reimbursement for lost wages and work benefits caused by the acts of the employer.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 6310, subd. (c) — family-member retaliation (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: An employer, or a person acting on behalf of the employer, shall not retaliate against an employee because the employee is a family member of a person who has, or is perceived to have, engaged in any acts protected by this section.
